title: Add `athena drain`: run the queue within a budget, report the stop
summary: Add a CLI command that works through queued requests (steward- and audience-queued) itself: run each job to its end, land it and rate it, until the target check passes or a user-set USD/job budget is spent. It then prints why it stopped. The audience is the repository owner, who today runs `go`, `land` and rating by hand for each item.

defaults_applied.how: One new command and one core module that reuse the existing go/land/score paths.
Fake-agent tests cover the stop reasons: target met, budget spent, empty queue, needs a person.
The budget limit is enforced in code before each job starts and is pinned by a test, not left as prose.
I took the unstated target, budget source and rating step from the steward and score code and read them as the assumptions above.
Help text, docs and the stop report are written for an outside reader.
A verifier exercises the command through cargo test and cargo run -- drain --help.
BRIEF.md asks for tagged releases and a changelog, so the change records itself in CHANGELOG.md.

assumptions: The budget is given on the command line (`--budget-usd`, optional `--max-jobs`), not in athena.toml, so no governance file changes.
'The outcome you are working toward' is the steward's target: the queue is empty and a fresh steward pass raises no new finding. The loop re-runs that check after each job.
Each item reuses the existing go/land/score paths (go_and_report, land, score); the loop adds no new way to land.

Spend is the sum of recorded job costs from the records for jobs the loop ran; the loop checks it before starting each job and never starts one once the remaining budget is below the configured per-job cap or zero.
Items that need a person (proposals above the role's ladder limit, e.g. accept-proposal / approve-work) are not decided by the loop; it stops or skips them and reports them.
A job that is rejected or fails is recorded and counted. The loop stops after a repeat failure of the same item instead of retrying forever.
The 'rate' step means the existing scoring of the result (score/jev); the loop invokes it and does not invent a new rating.
question: What is the 'outcome you are working toward' that ends the loop? I assumed the queue is empty and a fresh steward pass finds nothing new. Say so if you mean something else, such as a named check.

acceptance_criteria.text: `cargo test` passes, including new tests with the fake agent for: (a) a queue of two requests both run and landed, with the stop reason 'target met'; (b) a budget too small for the next job, with the stop reason 'budget spent' and the remaining items left queued; (c) an empty queue, which stops at once without spending.
Running the new command with `--help` (`cargo run -p athena-cli -- drain --help`) documents the budget flags and the possible stop reasons.
The loop never starts a job when the recorded spend plus the next job's cap would exceed the budget. A unit test pins this, and it holds even when a job reports a cost above its estimate.

The command's final output (text and `--json`) names the stop reason (target met, budget spent, job limit, needs a person, repeated failure), the jobs run with their outcomes and costs, the total spent, and the items still queued. The owner can read where it stopped without opening records.
Items that need a person are never accepted, approved or landed by the loop on the person's behalf; a test shows an above-ladder proposal is listed as waiting and left untouched.
README or docs and CHANGELOG describe the command, its budget semantics, and what it deliberately does not decide. A decisions entry records the choice not to add a config key.

out_of_scope: Changing the athena.toml budget keys or any other governance file.
Auto-accepting steward proposals or work items above the role's ladder limit.
Changing how the verifier, the landing gate or scoring work.
Scheduling the loop in the background or from CI.
departures: This is a new multi-module feature with a loop over existing run/land/score paths and an ambiguous 'target'. That puts cost, time and acceptance risk above the reference, which is built mostly from smaller changes.
